design_detail: Monograph in Psychological Science in the Public Interest (vol. 8, no. 2, pp. 53–96; 11 tables, 16 figures) by a team of psychologists and physicians: Gerd Gigerenzer, Wolfgang Gaissmaier and Elke Kurz-Milcke (Max Planck Institute for Human Development and Harding Center for Risk Literacy, Berlin) and Lisa M. Schwartz and Steven Woloshin (Center for Medicine and the Media, Dartmouth Institute for Health Policy and Clinical Practice). It argues that patients, journalists and physicians commonly misunderstand health statistics, which the authors call collective statistical illiteracy; that confusing forms of presenting numbers (relative risks, conditional probabilities such as sensitivity and specificity, 5-year survival rates, single-event probabilities) cause much of this and are sometimes used to persuade; and that transparent forms (absolute risks, natural frequencies, mortality rates, frequency statements), better reporting and teaching statistical thinking from primary school onwards are the remedy. Seven parts: three opening cases; a definition of minimal statistical literacy with questions to ask about any risk; evidence on patients, journalists and physicians; consequences; causes (historical and institutional, including conflicts of interest); remedies; conclusion. The evidence is a selection of surveys, experiments and content analyses, many by the authors themselves and some unpublished, together with continuing-education sessions run by the first author and anecdotes; for patients the authors call it not an exhaustive overview but an analysis of the main issues (p. 60). No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal of the cited studies, and no pooling: a narrative review, read with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: What these authors argued about how health statistics are misunderstood and presented, and what the studies they cite reported as they summarize them, including experiments in which the same numbers were misjudged more often when given as relative risks or conditional probabilities than as absolute risks or natural frequencies.
cannot_establish: How common these misunderstandings are among people who use drugs or readers of drug information (no cited study concerns drug information or drug use), how complete or representative the cited evidence is (no search; several central figures are unpublished or come from the first author's courses), or how large the framing effects are (Covey's meta-analysis is cited without its numbers).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited samples include: a representative sample of about 1,000 German citizens surveyed in 2006 (Figs. 6–7; Gigerenzer, 2008, unpublished); 450 US adults aged 35 to 70, described as nationally representative (Table 4); 85 physicians at grand rounds (Table 7); 178 people recruited through newspaper advertisements, an outpatient clinic and a hospital open house (Table 5); 160 and 150 gynecologists attending the first author's continuing-education courses (pp. 55, 70); 48 physicians (Hoffrage & Gigerenzer, 1998); 306 New Zealand telephone respondents (Sarfati et al., 1998); content analyses of news stories, press releases, journal articles, pamphlets, invitation letters, web sites and pharmaceutical leaflets (Tables 6 and 9; pp. 66–67, 77–80).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selected by the authors, with a large share from their own groups (natural-frequency studies by Gigerenzer and Hoffrage; numeracy, media and press-release studies by Schwartz and Woloshin) and from unpublished data; several samples are convenience samples (course attendees, clinic visitors). Most examples concern cancer screening, in the US, Germany and the UK; none concerns drugs used outside medicine.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. In the cited experiments the 'exposure' is the format in which the same numbers are given (relative or absolute risk, conditional probabilities or natural frequencies, single-event or frequency statements).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. In the cited experiments, the same information presented in a different format.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: numeracy questions (Tables 3, 4 and 7), the medical data interpretation test (Table 5), multiple-choice and open estimates of positive predictive value and of what a relative reduction means (Figs. 2, 7, 9 and 10), willingness to accept a test or fund a programme, and counts of features in news stories, press releases, journal articles and patient materials (Tables 6 and 9).
outcomes.operationalization: Minimal statistical literacy in health is defined by a list of insights and questions (pp. 58–60); a format is called transparent according to the proportion of a population that understands it correctly, which the authors say depends on expertise (p. 77).

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no pooling); the percentages and counts of the cited studies are given in key_findings as the monograph summarizes them. Editors' calculations for the authors' examples: contraceptive pill, 1 against 2 in 7,000 is an absolute increase of about 0.014 percentage points behind a relative increase of 100%; Lipitor advertisement (Fig. 11), 2.8% against 1.5% over 4 years is 13 fewer strokes per 1,000 and a relative reduction of about 46%.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. A contrary finding (Sheridan et al., 2003: relative risk reductions led to more correct answers) is cited and attributed to awkward phrasing of the absolute risks (p. 65); the Caution section (p. 90) reports that absolute numbers can lead people to dismiss small but important effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Selected surveys and experiments in which many patients, physicians and other professionals misread relative risks, conditional probabilities and survival rates and did better with absolute risks and natural frequencies, and content analyses in which news stories, press releases, journal articles and patient materials often gave relative risks without absolute numbers, omitted harms or omitted limitations.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says the authors provide evidence that statistical illiteracy is common to patients, journalists and physicians, is created by nontransparent framing, sometimes intentionally, and can have serious consequences for health (p. 53). The general term collective statistical illiteracy rests on selected and partly convenience samples, several unpublished, without a search. The causes in Part V (paternalism, determinism, conflicts of interest) are argued historically and illustrated, not tested. The 13,000 additional abortions attributed to the 1995 pill scare (p. 54) rest on one secondary source and on the reversal of a downward trend after the alert (Fig. 1), a before–after association. The authors themselves warn that absolute numbers can lead people to dismiss effects that are small but important (p. 90).

timeline.event: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage show that natural frequencies, but not relative frequencies, make probability judgements easier (as cited, pp. 56, 90).
Hoffrage and Gigerenzer: 48 physicians estimate positive predictive values far better from natural frequencies than from conditional probabilities (as cited, pp. 68–69).
Woloshin and Schwartz: press releases often fail to quantify the main effect, give relative risks without base rates and omit limitations (as cited, p. 67).
Schwartz, Woloshin, Dvorin and Welch: 68% of 222 articles in leading journals do not give the absolute risks for the first ratio measure in the abstract (as cited, p. 77).
Covey's meta-analysis of experiments on presenting treatment benefits in different formats (as cited, pp. 65, 70).
Sumner et al. on exaggeration in academic press releases and the news stories that follow, on file and read by another first reader in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited synthesis by researchers who developed several of the remedies it recommends. Its conclusions about formats rest mainly on experiments by the authors' groups and on Covey's meta-analysis (cited without numbers); its figures on media, press releases and journals come from content analyses that should be cited from the primary studies where possible. For the site's 'Seven questions': it supports question 5 most directly (relative risks without base rates mislead; give absolute numbers in both groups) and question 7 (news stories, press releases, journal abstracts and pharmaceutical leaflets often omit absolute numbers, harms or limitations), and bears on question 1 through its question 'Does it apply to me?' and on 'linked to is not causes' through the finding that only 10% of news stories on uncontrolled studies said the outcome could not be tied to the exposure. It adds a qualification to question 5: absolute numbers need context, or small but important effects may be dismissed. It touches question 4 only in passing (equating the p-value with the probability that the null hypothesis is true is listed as a textbook error) and says nothing about measurements before use (2), doses (3) or replication (6).

funding.funder: Not reported. The acknowledgments thank eight colleagues for comments (p. 90); the copyright line names the Association for Psychological Science (p. 53).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors developed and promote several of the remedies they recommend: natural frequencies (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage) and the drug facts box (Schwartz, Woloshin and Welch), tested in the authors' own two studies (p. 86). The first author trained about 1,000 gynecologists and some 100 German science writers in risk communication, and Schwartz and Woloshin teach journalists (pp. 55, 67). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For drug information specifically: randomized comparisons, among people who use drugs and readers of drug information, of the same risk given as a relative risk ('twice the risk'), as absolute frequencies in both groups and with a familiar comparison, measuring understanding and decisions; and a systematic review of framing experiments with pooled effect sizes.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the patient section is described as not an exhaustive overview (p. 60).
Sample sizes and designs are usually given and representative samples are named as such, but no study is appraised; several figures are unpublished, from course attendees, or anecdotes.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Much of the central evidence comes from the authors' own studies, unpublished data and teaching sessions (for example Figs. 2, 6, 7, 9 and 10; Tables 4, 5, 7 and 10; the press-release and media studies).
Data and argument are mostly distinguishable, but the causal account (Part V) and some consequences (the abortion figure, p. 54) are presented with more certainty than the cited evidence allows.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how well people understand different formats (studies in which relative risks or conditional probabilities were understood as well, or better, are few)
domains.note: One contrary study is cited and explained away (p. 65); the Caution section (p. 90) gives a real counterpoint about absolute numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The overall 'high' follows the rule that it can be no milder than the worst domain (no search; heavy reliance on the authors' own work) and does not dispute the arithmetic of the examples, which is checkable. Cite the monograph for its arguments and worked examples (relative against absolute risk, survival against mortality, natural frequencies), labelling figures from cited studies as second-hand; anchor key numbers (press releases, news stories, journal abstracts) in the primary studies where possible.

key_findings.finding: 1995 contraceptive pill scare: the UK Committee on Safety of Medicines warned that third-generation pills doubled ('100%') the risk of potentially life-threatening blood clots; in the studies behind the warning, about 1 in 7,000 women on second-generation pills and 2 in 7,000 on third-generation pills had a thrombosis, an absolute increase of 1 in 7,000. The authors attribute to the scare an estimated 13,000 additional abortions in England and Wales in the following year, with some 800 additional conceptions in girls under 16 (Furedi, 1999).
key_findings.locator: I. Statistical Illiteracy in Patients, Physicians, and Politicians › The Contraceptive Pill Scare, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 5: 'twice the risk' here was 2 against 1 in 7,000. The abortion figure is second-hand and rests on a reversal of the downward trend after the alert (Fig. 1), not on an analysis that rules out other causes.

key_findings.finding: Same relative change, very different importance: a drug lowering risk from 20% to 10% and one lowering it from 0.0002% to 0.0001% both give a 50% relative risk reduction; a 50% relative reduction fits a fall from 200 to 100 in 10,000 patients as well as from 2 to 1 in 10,000; the relative risk can be derived from absolute risks, but not the reverse. The authors recommend giving the absolute risk in each group (for example from 20 in 100 to 10 in 100 over 10 years), or frequencies (for every 100 people treated, 10 fewer events), and note that 'percent lower' is ambiguous between relative and absolute.
key_findings.locator: III › Do Journalists Help the Public to Understand Health Statistics? › Nontransparent Numbers, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 66); V › Do Medical Journals Provide Transparent Information?, 3rd paragraph (p. 78)
key_findings.note: Supports the site's question 5 ('Out of how many?').

key_findings.finding: What a 25% relative reduction means: the authors equate the 25% reduction in breast cancer deaths attributed to mammography screening with about 1 fewer death per 1,000 women; asked about it, the most frequent answer in a representative sample of 1,000 German citizens was 500 fewer per 1,000 (Fig. 7); of 150 gynecologists on a course, 66% chose 1, 16% 25, 3% 100 and 15% 250 per 1,000; in random samples of women in four countries only 6% gave an absolute reduction between 0 and 5 per 1,000, and 60%, 44%, 37% and 37% (United States, Italy, United Kingdom, Switzerland) believed it was 80 or more per 1,000.
key_findings.locator: Summary, 1st paragraph (p. 53); III › Do Patients Understand Health Statistics? › Understanding That Screening Tests May Have Benefits and Harms, 1st paragraph (p. 63, continuing on p. 64) and Fig. 7 (p. 64); III › Do Physicians Understand Health Statistics? › Relative Risk Reductions Can Cause Exaggerated Perceptions of Treatment Effects, 2nd paragraph with its list of answers (p. 70)
key_findings.note: The German survey is cited to an unpublished manuscript (Gigerenzer, 2008) and the gynecologists were course attendees with no published source; the 1-in-1,000 figure is the authors' estimate, not data shown in the monograph, and Table 11 (p. 89) uses a different illustrative pair (about 20%, from about 5 to about 4 per 1,000).

key_findings.finding: Framing experiments: when the same benefit of a screening test was given as a relative reduction (about one third over 10 years), 80% of 306 New Zealand respondents said they would likely accept it, against 53% when given as an absolute reduction (from about 3 to about 2 in 1,000 over 10 years) and 43% as a number needed to screen (1 life saved per 1,000 screened every 10 years) (Sarfati et al., 1998); 87% of health professionals at diabetes conferences (160 nurse educators, 112 physicians and 27 others) judged a prevention effect important when given as a relative reduction, 39% when given as the corresponding glucose values (Mühlhauser et al., 2006); only 3 of 140 health-authority reviewers noticed that four funding proposals giving the same benefit in different forms were equivalent, and the relative version was seen as most deserving (Fahey et al., 1995); a meta-analysis included 13 experiments with physicians and 3 with other health professionals (Covey, 2007).
key_findings.locator: III › Do Patients Understand Health Statistics? › Understanding the Difference Between Relative and Absolute Risk Reduction, 1st paragraph, after its bulleted list (p. 65); III › Do Physicians Understand Health Statistics? › Relative Risk Reductions Can Cause Exaggerated Perceptions of Treatment Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 69, continuing on p. 70), 3rd paragraph (p. 70, from 'British researchers') and 4th paragraph (p. 70)
key_findings.note: Second-hand. Covey's pooled results are not given.

key_findings.finding: News stories (Table 6): benefits of newly approved medications were quantified in 7% of US newspaper stories on ropinirole (n = 15), 21% of 357 Norwegian stories on 18 medications and 20% of 193 Canadian stories on five medications; where quantified, they were given only as a relative risk reduction in 0%, 89% and 39%; harms were mentioned in 29%, 39% and 32%. For other medications and interventions: 200 US newspaper and television stories, 60% quantified, 83% relative only, 47% harms; 50 Australian stories, 40%, not applicable, 44%; 187 international news reports on research from five scientific meetings, 60%, 35%, 29%.
key_findings.locator: III › Do Journalists Help the Public to Understand Health Statistics? › No Numbers, 1st paragraph (p. 65, continuing on p. 66); Table 6 (p. 66)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's questions 5 and 7. 'Relative risk reduction only' is a percentage of the stories in which the benefit was quantified (Table 6 note).

key_findings.finding: Limitations and press releases: in coverage of research presented at five scientific meetings, only 10% of stories about uncontrolled studies noted that it was impossible to know whether the outcome really related to the exposure (Woloshin & Schwartz, 2006b); press releases did not quantify the main effect in 35%, gave relative risks without base rates in 45% of those reporting differences between study groups, and made no note of study limitations in 77% (Woloshin & Schwartz, 2002).
key_findings.locator: III › Do Journalists Help the Public to Understand Health Statistics? › No Cautions, 1st paragraph (p. 66, continuing on p. 67) and 2nd paragraph (p. 67)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 7 ('Does the summary say more than the data?') and on 'linked to is not causes'. Sample sizes of the two cited studies are not given in the monograph.

key_findings.finding: Journal articles: of 359 reports of randomized trials published in 1989, 1992, 1995 and 1998 in five leading journals, only 25 reported the absolute risk reduction (14 of them also the number needed to treat), about 7% (Nuovo et al., 2002); in 2003/2004, 68% of 222 articles in the same journals and the Journal of the National Cancer Institute did not give the absolute risks for the first ratio measure in the abstract, and about half of these did not give them anywhere in the article (Schwartz et al., 2006); in BMJ, JAMA and The Lancet 2004–2006, about half of articles did not report absolute risks or other transparent frequencies, and when both benefits and harms were reported, 1 in 3 studies used mismatched framing, usually relative risks for benefits and absolute frequencies for harms (Sedrakyan & Shih, 2007).
key_findings.locator: V. Causes of Statistical Illiteracy › Do Medical Journals Provide Transparent Information?, 1st paragraph (p. 77) and 2nd paragraph (p. 78)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's questions 5 and 7: the numbers that headlines inflate often already lack absolute risks in the journal abstract. The 68% is printed in words (sixty-eight percent).

key_findings.finding: Leaflets and patient materials: researchers who compared 175 pharmaceutical advertising leaflets for doctors with the original studies could verify the leaflets' summaries in only 8% of cases; in the other 92%, key results were often distorted or important details omitted (Kaiser et al., 2004). A leaflet gave hormone replacement therapy's benefit as protection against colorectal cancer 'by up to more than 50 percent' and its harm as a possible breast cancer increase of 0.6 percent (6 in 1,000); the authors find the benefit in absolute terms to be under 6 in 1,000, and of 80 women aged 41 to 69 given the leaflet, 75% wrongly understood that the therapy prevents more cancers than it causes and 4% understood the opposite (Hoffrage, 2003).
key_findings.locator: V › Are Patients Likely to Find Transparent Information in Medical Pamphlets and Web Sites? › Pamphlets, 2nd paragraph (p. 79); V › How Accurate Are Leaflets Distributed to Doctors?, 1st paragraph (p. 80)
key_findings.note: Mismatched framing (benefit relative, harm absolute) bears on the site's questions 5 and 7.

key_findings.finding: Survival is not mortality: with screening, 5-year survival rises even if no death is delayed, through lead time (diagnosed at 67 and dying at 70 gives 0% 5-year survival; diagnosed at 60 by screening and still dying at 70 gives 100%) and overdiagnosis (1,000 men with progressive cancer, 440 alive after 5 years, 44%; adding 2,000 screen-detected non-progressive cancers gives 2,440 of 3,000, 81%, with the same 560 deaths). Over 50 years, changes in 5-year survival for the 20 most common solid tumours in the United States were uncorrelated with changes in mortality (correlation 0.0; Welch et al., 2000); prostate cancer 5-year survival was 98% in the United States and 71% in Britain, but mortality about 26 and 27 per 100,000 men (Shibata & Whittemore, 2001).
key_findings.locator: I › Higher Survival Does Not Mean Longer Life, 4th paragraph (p. 56, continuing on p. 57), 5th paragraph (p. 57) and 7th–8th paragraphs (p. 57); Figs. 4–5 (p. 57)
key_findings.note: The 2,440 of 3,000 and the 560 deaths are printed in Fig. 5, not in the running text. Not about drugs, but a general case of a number that looks like benefit and is not; the lead-time and overdiagnosis examples are hypothetical.

key_findings.finding: Positive tests and natural frequencies: told that 1% of women screened have breast cancer, that 90% of them test positive and that 9% of the others also test positive, only 21% of 160 gynecologists chose the best answer, that about 1 in 10 women with a positive mammogram has cancer (most answered 90% or 81%; estimates ranged from 1% to 90%); after training in natural frequencies (10 in 1,000 have cancer, 9 of them test positive, and about 89 of the 990 without cancer also test positive), 87% did. In a study of 48 physicians, estimates of the chance of colorectal cancer after a positive stool test ranged from 1% to 99% with conditional probabilities and were mostly correct with natural frequencies (Hoffrage & Gigerenzer, 1998). For heterosexual men at low risk, with a base rate of about 1 in 10,000, the chance that a positive HIV test (ELISA and Western blot) means infection can be as low as 50%.
key_findings.locator: I › Few Gynecologists Understand Positive Mammograms, 2nd–5th paragraphs and Figs. 2–3 (pp. 55–56); III › Do Physicians Understand Health Statistics? › The Illusion of Certainty, 1st paragraph (p. 67); › Physicians Are Confused by Sensitivities and Specificities, 1st–2nd paragraphs and Fig. 9 (pp. 68–69)
key_findings.note: Bears on reading screening results, including drug tests (a positive screen in a group where few have the condition may often be a false positive); the gynecologist audiences are course attendees with no published source.

key_findings.finding: Numeracy: in 450 US adults aged 35 to 70 (Table 4), 70% converted 1% to 10 in 1,000, 25% converted 1 in 1,000 to 0.1% and 76% estimated how many heads come up in 1,000 coin flips; in the highest education groups at most 30% could do the second task. Among 85 physicians at grand rounds (Table 7) the figures were 91%, 75% and 100%, and 72% answered all three correctly. On the medical data interpretation test (178 participants, Table 5), 81% knew that a comparison group is needed to decide whether a benefit exists, 63% that the base rate is needed in addition to the relative risk, 45% that denominators are needed to compare risks in two groups, and 20% that lower all-cause mortality is better evidence of benefit than lower deaths from one cause.
key_findings.locator: III › Do Patients Understand Health Statistics? › Basic Numeracy, 2nd paragraph and Table 4 (p. 61); › Medical Data Interpretation Test, 1st paragraph (p. 61) and Table 5 (p. 62); III › Do Physicians Understand Health Statistics? › Basic Numeracy, 1st paragraph and Table 7 (p. 67)
key_findings.note: Table 4's stated source does not match the reference list (reporting_issues).

key_findings.finding: Questions everyone should ask about any risk (the authors' minimal statistical literacy): risk of what (the outcome); time frame; how big, in absolute terms or compared with a familiar risk; does it apply to me, that is, is it based on studies of people like you in age, sex or health problems; and, about the science behind the numbers, the quality of evidence (randomized trials, then well-designed cohort or case-control studies, then expert opinion) and what conflicts of interest exist.
key_findings.locator: II. What Is Statistical Literacy? › Minimal Statistical Literacy in Health › Questions to Ask About All Risks (p. 58); › Questions About the Science Behind the Numbers (p. 60)
key_findings.note: Parallels the site's questions 1 ('Who was studied?') and 5 ('Out of how many?').

key_findings.finding: Single-event statements mislead: a psychiatrist who told patients they had a 30 to 50% chance of a sexual problem on Prozac found that many understood something would go wrong in 30 to 50% of their sexual encounters; saying that 3 to 5 of every 10 patients who take Prozac have a sexual problem made patients less anxious (Gigerenzer, 2002).
key_findings.locator: VI. Therapy › Transparency › Transparent Numbers, paragraph beginning 'Similarly, when in clinical practice' (p. 88, continuing on p. 89); Table 11 (p. 89)
key_findings.note: An anecdote reported by the first author; the frequency format is the authors' recommendation.

key_findings.finding: A drug facts box as a model of transparent numbers (Table 10, from Schwartz, Woloshin & Welch, 2007): for tamoxifen, in 13,000 women at high risk given the drug or a sugar pill for 5 years, invasive breast cancer 3.3% against 1.7% (16 in 1,000 fewer), no difference in breast cancer deaths (about 0.9 in 1,000), blood clots 0.5% against 1.0%, invasive uterine cancer 0.5% against 1.1%, cataracts needing surgery 1.5% against 2.3%, and no difference in deaths from all causes (about 12 in 1,000), each given in percentages and per 1,000 for both groups.
key_findings.note: A format for presenting benefits and harms side by side in absolute numbers; the authors tested it in two of their own studies (p. 86).

key_findings.finding: An advertisement claiming that atorvastatin (Lipitor) cuts the risk of stroke by nearly half (48%) is shown beside the absolute figures: after 4 years, 2.8% of patients taking a sugar pill and 1.5% of those taking the drug had a stroke.
key_findings.note: The 48% is printed in the advertisement reproduced in the figure. Editors' calculation: 13 fewer strokes per 1,000 over 4 years, a relative reduction of about 46%. The figure's own commentary rounds the relative claim to 50%.

key_findings.finding: Caution from the authors: accurate, balanced numbers can make people dismiss small but important effects; in one of their studies, participants' optimism dropped about equally for three drugs after seeing the data, including a statin that lowered overall mortality over 5 years from 4 in 100 to 3 in 100, a reduction the authors say few drugs match; people need context on the size of benefits of other interventions.
key_findings.note: Says something more than the site's question 5: an absolute difference that looks small can still matter, so absolute numbers need a comparison.

key_findings.finding: Errors found in textbooks and journals include equating the positive predictive value with the sensitivity, and the p-value with the probability that the null hypothesis is correct.
key_findings.locator: VI › Teach Statistical Literacy in Medical Training, 2nd paragraph, after the quotation from Healy
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4: the same error the ASA statement warns against (sc_wasserstein_2016, principle 2).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 (450 US adults, said to be a nationally representative sample) and Table 7 (85 physicians at grand rounds) are both attributed to Schwartz and Woloshin (2000), and the reference list describes that source only as a physician grand round survey, unpublished data. The education subgroups of Table 4 (131, 151, 103 and 62) do not add up to the 450 overall (editors' sum: 447).
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the population numeracy figures cannot be traced or checked from the monograph; cite them as unpublished data reported by the authors.

reporting_issues.issue: Several central figures rest on unpublished sources or on unreferenced sessions: the German surveys on certainty of tests (Fig. 6) and on what a 25% reduction means (Fig. 7) cite Gigerenzer (2008), an unpublished manuscript; the economists' and seven-country surveys are unpublished manuscripts; the 160 and 150 gynecologists were attendees of the first author's courses, with no reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: These results have not been peer reviewed as reported; a claim should label them as the authors' unpublished data.

reporting_issues.issue: The German survey on tests is described as a nationwide survey of 1,000 citizens over 18 in the text and as a representative sample of 1,016 in the legend of Fig. 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample size should be given as about 1,000.

reporting_issues.issue: Giuliani's British figures are given as 49 men per 100,000 diagnosed, of whom 28 died within 5 years, about 44%; the 44% is close to the share who survived, not the share who died (editors' calculation: 21 of 49 survived, 43%; 28 of 49 died, 57%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor ambiguity: the 44% is a survival figure, consistent with the 82% survival quoted for the United States.

reporting_issues.issue: The illustrative relative reduction for mammography differs within the monograph: 25% meaning about 1 in 1,000 (Summary and pp. 63–64, 70) against about 20%, from about 5 to about 4 in 1,000 (Table 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: both are rounded illustrations implying different baseline risks; a claim should cite one consistently and as approximate.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record as downloaded from the publisher's site), pp. 53–96 (all 44 pages: text, Tables 1–11, Figs. 1–16 and their legends, acknowledgments and reference list; every number on the card checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Fig. 6 also at 300 dpi; no supplement). The PDF prints volume 8, number 2 and a 2008 copyright line, but no issue date.
